cards.name: Day and night
cards.text: In US cities, daytime temperatures run about 1 to 7°F higher than in outlying areas, and nighttime temperatures about 2 to 5°F higher.

cards.name: Roofs
cards.text: On a warm day, ordinary roofing can reach as much as 66°F warmer than the air around it.

cards.name: Trees
cards.text: Trees and plants cool streets two ways: shade, and water evaporating from their leaves.

cards.name: Tons
cards.text: In 2010, an estimated 4.8 to 12.7 million metric tons of plastic washed into the ocean from land.

cards.name: Most common
cards.text: Plastic is the most common kind of trash found in the ocean and on beaches.

cards.name: Smaller
cards.text: Plastic does not rot away. It breaks into smaller and smaller pieces; under 5 mm, they are called microplastics.

cards.name: Decline
cards.text: Monarch numbers have been falling steadily since the mid-1990s.

cards.name: Winter
cards.text: Eastern monarchs spend the winter packed into fir forests in the mountains of central Mexico.

traditions.name: Vanitas still life
traditions.intro: Painters filled tables with beautiful things and quiet warnings. Every object reminds the viewer that life and wealth do not last.
traits: Symbols of time running out (a snuffed candle, an hourglass)
Things at the edge of decay (wilting flowers, peeled fruit)
A dark plain background with one strong window light
Costly objects shown in loving detail

traditions.name: Ukiyo-e woodblock prints
traditions.intro: Prints of famous places, seasons and city life, carved on wood with one block for each color. Artists sold them in series, like Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (about 1830 to 1832).
traits: Flat areas of color with bold outlines
A big shape close up, framing a small far view
A place shown in a season or weather
Prussian blue, a new imported blue printmakers took up around 1830

traditions.name: WPA posters
traditions.intro: During the Great Depression, a government program paid artists to make posters for parks, health, safety and community events. Most were silkscreen prints, so each design could be printed many times.
traits: Flat layered colors, a few at a time
Simple strong shapes that read from far away
Made to be printed many times and posted in public

pages.text: The beach near my aunt's house is half plastic after a storm.
Vanitas paintings warn you about things that last too short. Plastic is the opposite: it lasts too long.
A heap on the beach. A skull built of bottles. A table with a fish and a plastic bag.

tags.note: Tons is too big to draw. One table of it is something people can look at.
tags.label: Tons

tags.note: A table, like the Dutch painters
tags.label: Costly objects shown in loving detail

pages.text: A value study: one bottle, one shell, one window.

tags.note: Dark back, one window light. It makes plain trash look precious.
tags.label: A dark plain background with one strong window light

pages.text: Replace the skull with a fish skeleton tangled in a bag.

tags.note: Not a human skull. The warning is about the fish.
tags.label: Symbols of death (a skull)

tags.note: The bag, because it is the thing I find most.
tags.label: Most common

pages.text: A lighter instead of a candle. Bright caps against the dark.

tags.note: Their candle burns out. My lighter never goes away.
tags.label: Symbols of time running out (a snuffed candle, an hourglass)

tags.note: Bright plastic colors against the dark, so the trash is the loudest thing.
tags.label: My own idea

pages.text: A Dutch vanitas warns that beautiful things don't last. My still life warns about the things that last too long. I borrowed the dark table and window light, but swapped the skull for a fish and the candle for a lighter.

tags.note: Painted on a cardboard box from a delivery, so the painting is made of packaging too.
tags.label: My own idea

tags.note: Tiny bright specks in the sand at the front: the pieces you can't pick up.
tags.label: Smaller
